_provenance.source_pdf: Benson, George - The George Benson Method, Vol 5 (Melodic Minor World, Bebop Scales, Symmetric Ideas & Concepts).pdf

usage_notes.narrative: For Gsus(b9), Benson prescribes deriving single lines from the melodic minor scale a whole step below the sus root: 'Over a Gsus(b9) we would visualize the single lines as being derived from "F" melodic minor because the Gsus(b9) chord is the IInd degree of the F melodic minor scale.' The player locates the sus(b9) chord as degree II of the parent melodic minor, then uses that parent scale as the improvisation source. Chapter 5, p. 15.

For C#7alt, Benson prescribes visualizing single lines from the melodic minor scale a half step above the altered dominant root: 'Over a C#7alt we would visualize the single lines as being derived from "D" melodic minor because the C# altered is the VIIth degree of the D melodic minor scale.' The altered dominant is located as degree VII of the parent melodic minor, and that scale governs improvisation. Chapter 5, p. 15.

For C+maj7 (augmented major seventh), Benson prescribes deriving lines from either A melodic minor or C Ionian(#5): 'Over a C+maj7 we would visualize the single lines as being derived from "A" melodic minor or "C" Ionian (#5) because it is the IIIrd degree (relative) of A melodic minor.' The aug-maj7 chord sits at degree III, and the Lydian(#5)/melodic minor pairing is the characteristic scale resource. Chapter 5, p. 15.

For Am(maj7) -- the tonic minor-major seventh -- Benson prescribes using it as one of the two master guide chord shapes anchoring all five fretboard zones: 'we can use the same 5 vertical zones exactly as we did before with Ionian and Aeolian but this time having Cmaj7(#5) and Am(maj7) as guiding chords.' All melodic minor tetrads across the neck must be related back to this shape. Additionally, the full tension set must be known even if not all tensions are voiced: 'we have to know all of them in order to do not make a mistake when harmonizing or improvising.' Chapter 5, p. 15 (guide chord); Chapter 7, pp. 28, 33.

For Cmaj7(#5) -- the Lydian(#5) major seventh sharp-five -- Benson prescribes using it as the alternating guide chord alongside Am(maj7) in the five-zone fretboard system: 'Guide Chords -> Lydian (#5) & Melodic Minor = Cmaj7(#5) & Am(maj7). 1st Zone: Cmaj7(#5). 2nd Zone: Am(maj7). 3rd Zone: Cmaj7(#5).' Every zone on the neck alternates between these two shapes. Chapter 5, p. 15; Chapter 7, p. 33.

For D7(9) -- the dominant ninth used as the primary laboratory chord throughout the volume -- Benson prescribes applying melodic minor Giant Lines to create 'flux and reflux': extended melodic minor lines are run over the static D7(9) vamp to generate harmonic tension and release. The fretboard visualization for extended lines over this chord requires a minimum of two guide chords: 'we must use at least 2 guide chords in order to properly visualize what we are doing.' Chapters 3, 5, 7-9.

Do not attempt to visualize extended melodic minor scale options over a dominant seventh using only a single guide chord -- 'in these cases we must use at least 2 guide chords in order to properly visualize what we are doing.' A single anchor is explicitly ruled insufficient whenever the scale palette goes beyond basic options. Chapter 7, p. 27.

For D7(#11) specifically, Benson warns that its dual identity as both melodic minor IV and a dominant diminished voicing means certain scales and chords cannot safely be used over it: 'we must know that in some cases we cannot use certain types of scales and chords, otherwise we might have a terrible result.' The dual identity constrains the scale options. Chapter 7, p. 28.

For E7(9, b13) and D7(9, #11, 13) -- the melodic minor V and IV dominant chords -- Benson prescribes knowing all tensions completely even when voicing only a subset: 'The chords D7(9,#11,13), E7(9,b13) do not have to contain all the tensions presented. However, we have to know all of them in order to do not make a mistake when harmonizing or improvising.' Chapter 7, p. 28.

For Dm7 (and the Cm7 reference key used to teach it), Benson prescribes learning all melodic minor tetrads and Giant Lines by first anchoring them in the key of Cm: 'we will learn this new scale arpeggios in the key of "Cm" thus helping us to visualize the "Eb" note replacing "E" note.' The minor seventh chord shape serves as the visual anchor for the Eb/E substitution. Chapters 7, 11, 13.

For F#o (half-diminished, the sixth degree of A melodic minor), Benson prescribes deriving improvisation lines from the A melodic minor scale family: 'The next scale arpeggios can be applyed over any chord derived from "A" melodic minor scale: Am(maj7) or Am6, Bsus(b9), Cmaj7(#5), *D7(9,#11,13), *E7(9,b13), F#o, G#7alt.' The half-diminished chord is treated as an integral member of the melodic minor chord family. Chapter 7, pp. 28, 33.
